title: Dems' best Kansas Senate poll in 30+ years: Enten explains why
description:
According to new CNN polls, in deep-red Kansas, there is no clear leader between Democrat Adam Hamilton (49%) and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall (45%), even as likely voters there say they would prefer Republicans to control the Senate. Voters here largely view Marshall unfavorably and say their choices are about Marshall more so than Hamilton.

In Kansas, the most Republican-friendly of the four states polled, only about one-third hold a positive view of the Democratic Party. But Hamilton, like Talarico, is overperforming his party – even as he’s a lesser-known quantity. In this case, the more relevant number may be Marshall’s underperformance and unpopularity. Most likely voters say that they view the Republican nominee negatively, and a 59% majority of Hamilton’s backers say they’re motivated primarily by opposition to Marshall.

title: Could Latino voters cost Trump and Republicans Congress?
description:
Latinos have emerged in recent years as perhaps the biggest group of swing voters in the United States. And if results next month mirror polls that suggest the nation’s 36 million Latino voters are shifting in significant numbers in Democrats’ favor, those voters could be responsible for handing the party control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Traditionally a Democratic-leaning portion of the electorate in most of the nation, Latinos swung heavily toward Trump in the 2024 election — igniting Republican dreams of a long-term political realignment that could remake the American political map, particularly across the growing South.
But the economic frustrations that helped propel Trump to victory are now fueling dissatisfaction among many of those same voters with Republicans who fully control the federal government.

title: Trump called his new AI chatbot ‘damn good.’ Then it fact-checked him
description:
President Donald Trump launched a new artificial intelligence chatbot on Tuesday, calling it “damn good.” Turns out that one of the things it’s reasonably good at is debunking Trump’s own lies.

We asked the America.gov chatbot about numerous false claims the president has made in recent months, including one he uttered at the Tuesday launch event itself. The chatbot flatly and correctly noted that many of these Trump claims are not true – including assertions he has made about elections, the economy, immigration and foreign affairs.

The chatbot is not the best tool for political fact-checking. Intended to help Americans access federal information and services, it refused to address some Trump falsehoods on the grounds that the answers would require information from sources outside the federal government. It also provided outdated or incomplete evidence in some cases. Still, its firm rejections of some of his most frequent falsehoods represent a rare repudiation of his dishonesty from a source his administration developed and he personally endorsed.

title: Trump’s BLUE WAVE NIGHTMARE: Key investigation LOOMS
description:
After the historic repudiation of Donald Trump in the 2026 midterms, accountability is coming. Andrew Weissmann and Mary McCord break down the major rule-of-law issues likely to face investigation as Democrats take control of Congress — and explain just how much power the new Congress will have. The answer might surprise you.
They focus on two critical areas: oversight and spending, Congress’s ability to control the money.

Mary lays out the robust oversight coming for the Department of Justice, including who Democrats will want to hear from, particularly Todd Blanche. As well as other areas for probing — possible corruption, the alleged slush fund, potential abuses of power, and representations made by administration officials to Congress. 

They also dig into Trump’s vanity projects. Weissmann discusses why a judge temporarily halting the proposed arch over compliance with Congress could potentially stop the project for good.

UPDATE: After recording this episode, the House defeated Rep. Thomas Massie’s impeachment resolution against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. In a 211-204 vote, House Republicans were able to effectively kill the resolution by referring it to the Judiciary Committee. Rep. Massie was the sole Republican to vote with Democrats against the procedural move.

description:
MS NOW reporters Marc Santia and Jillian Frankel report on how Arizona law enforcement officials are implementing technology that uses existing infrastructure to keep voters safe on Election Day and beyond. The battleground state has long been the site of protests and false claims of stolen elections, and this year, the police officers in Apache Junction, near Phoenix, are leaving nothing to chance.

MS NOW got a look at how officers are using Peregrine Technologies to connect siloed streams of information, like 911 calls, body camera footage, and crime reports into a real-time dashboard. If there is an emergency or a disruption at a polling place, Peregrine says this dashboard will help police find the closest officer to the location and give supervisors faster information on how to address the situation. It also helps police avoid sending uniformed officers to stand guard at the polls, which could make voters uncomfortable.
